Examining the risks posed to the rule of law – both innocuous and sinister

By Alex Dean

March 5, 2021
Read this issue

In this review

FAKE LAW
The truth about justice in an age of lies 386pp. Picador. £20.
The Secret Barrister
Fake Law is a vital and timely examination of the risks to the rule of law when elements of the press connive with cynical politicians to exploit public ignorance. The anonymous author, whose first book on the criminal justice system, the field in which they practise, was a bestseller, has now cast their net wider. In this telling – which covers the whole justice system, from personal injury to high constitutional issues – journalists and politicians perform a sort of symbiotic dance, each goading the other into proclaiming more outrageous falsehoods about the law, which then gives both sides the cover to repeat them.

The Secret Barrister is a junior barrister specialising in criminal law, and part-time author and blogger.
The law can often feel to the public like an alien and impenetrable world, linked to everyday life only by selective news reportage and artistically-licensed tv dramatisation. This blog aims to bridge that gap by providing a candid, and hopefully accessible, explanation of our criminal justice system, of how it works, and of how, all too often, it doesn’t.

SB, as they're affectionately known, has become one the nation's most prominent critics of the government's eight-year cuts to legal aid and their damage done to the criminal justice system.
